newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-S.Africa rate hike seen reversed in Q2 97.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-S.Africa rate hike seen reversed in Q2 97.

text.p: A sharp slowdown in consumer spending coupled with lower economic growth should allow the South African authorities to reverse last week's one point hike in interest rates in the second quarter of 1997.
Over the next two years, interest rates are expected to be cut by up to five percentage points, according to the results of a Reuters survey published on Thursday.

Twenty of the 28 economists polled expected the prime overdraft rate -- currently 20.25 percent -- to be cut to 19.25 in the second quarter of 1997, followed by one further cut in the second half of next year.
In 1998, economists forecast up to three more cuts leaving prime at between 15 and 16.25 percent by the end of the year.

Economists said that by the second quarter, they expected the November 21 hike to have bitten deeply into burgeoning credit demand, cited by Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals as one of his main bugbears in the inflation conundrum.
"I think the credit bubble is going to burst," said Equisec economist Dawie Roodt, who was among a handful to predict a one point cut in both the first and second quarters of next year.

ABN AMRO economist Anastasia Gekis felt that government progress on its macro-economic strategy at the next budget, in March, would help interest rates lower as it boosted confidence and drew foreign investment back into the country.
JCI economist Peter Perkins also noted that the Reserve Bank's coincident indicator -- which measures the business cycle -- pointed to a rate cut in the second quarter.
Over the past 10 years, turning points in the indicator had lagged turning points in rates by about two years, he said.
"The coincident indicator started turning down at the beginning of the second quarter of 1995 and two years from then takes us to the second quarter of 1997 when we expect a rate cut," Perkins said.
Huysamer Stals economist Johan Rossouw said a sharp fall in inflation would also spur a decline in interest rates. He predicted three cuts of one point by the end of next year.
The Reuters survey forecast consumer price inflation would average at 8.94 percent in 1997 following an average of 7.48 percent in 1996.
Rossouw said he expected the consumer price index to fall to below six percent by the fourth quarter of next year.
"The fundamental argument is the fact that I do not expect the inflationary effect of the depreciation of the rand to be as high as is generally expected," he said.
"If you analyse (producer inflation) until now, the imported component has remained relatively flat despite the rand's depreciation."
Producer price inflation is expected to average 9.1 percent in 1997 from 7.2 percent this year.
Rand Merchant Bank Treasury economist Julia Roy noted that technical factors would also play an important role in inflation in coming months as next year's data would be calculated off a high base.
Econometrix economist Tony Twine was less sanguine about the prospects of lower inflation.
"Both producers and consumers have been cushioned from the decline in the rand probably by the extent of competition everywhere in the economy," he said.

"But sooner or later we believe that even the additional competitors will be faced with cost-push pressures...and that the price levels for both consumers and producers are going to be under more pressure for the next 12 to 18 months."
Frankel Pollak gilts analyst Tertia Jacobs said that in the short-term, rising inflation, tight money market conditions and the weak rand would hamper the bond market.
In the longer-term, however, she said with inflation expected to stage a turnaround going into the second half of 1997, bond yields would fall back.
The results of the survey show the yield on the R150 is expected to reach 15.44 percent in the first quarter of 1997 before moving to 14.52 percent by the end of next year.
